title: Factors Affecting Training and Physical Performance in Recreational Endurance Runners
authors: Boullosa D, Esteve-Lanao J, Casado A, Peyré-Tartaruga LA, Gomes da Rosa R, Del Coso J
population: Recreational endurance runners from novice to well-trained, drawn from studies of recreational and professional athletes; no participants of its own
findings: The review states that there is no consensus on the best practice for recreational runners to train for their objectives and improve performance in a healthy way, that much practice rests on anecdote ('10% rule', unvalidated monitoring algorithms, shoe types), and that most running evidence comes from studies of recreational and professional athletes of very different levels, which makes transfer to recreational runners difficult.

On intensity distribution it says that literature in recreational runners is scarce, so it is difficult to say which model is more beneficial; it names pyramidal and polarized as the forms to recommend, with different considerations by distance, time available and season, and ends with the advice that recreational runners should adopt a polarized distribution, although other models may also be beneficial, with at least 75% of time in zone 1 for better results.

It describes the trial of Muñoz et al. as finding that a polarized model improved 10 km performance more than a threshold model; the corpus record of that trial (munoz-2014-polarized-recreational) reports that the primary between-group difference was not significant (5.0% against 3.6%) and that the positive result came from a post-hoc subset.
On methods it recommends one to two high-intensity interval sessions a week plus more moderate and low continuous sessions, and a minimum effective dose of strength training.

On periodization it says research in recreational runners is very limited, that linear or block periodization may fit distances of 21 km or shorter, and, as 'a general recommendation from our practical experience', that marathons and longer events would probably benefit from reverse periodization, and novices from reverse periodization for 21 km or even 10 km; it adds that further studies are needed to test these suggestions.
limitations: A narrative review that names its basis as the authors' practical experience and gives no search method or appraisal of the studies it cites. Its advice is stronger than the studies it quotes (Muñoz 2014 above) and the reverse-periodization advice for marathons conflicts with a systematic review of reverse periodization that finds it no more effective than traditional periodization (gonzalezrave-2022-reverse-periodization; engine rule E1). Two authors are coaches or trainers (Esteve-Lanao's affiliation is a training-system company) and the paper declares no conflict of interest and no external funding. The statement of no consensus is as of 2020.
implications: Cite it for one claim: in 2020 its authors found no consensus on the best practice for recreational runners, and little recreational-runner evidence on intensity distribution or periodization.

Its recommendations (polarized for recreational runners, reverse periodization for marathons) are the authors' experience, conflict with E1 and the network meta-analysis (rosenblat-2025-tid-ipd-nma) and are no source for a rule, Param or preset.
